content: Anticholinergic medications function by inhibiting bronchoconstriction that is mediated through the vagus nerve. Additionally, they may reduce bronchial secretions. These agents have demonstrated efficacy in treating obstructive airway diseases and could potentially offer benefits in managing bronchiectasis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of anticholinergic therapy on both acute exacerbations and stable forms of bronchiectasis. To gather relevant data, the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register was thoroughly searched, and the bibliographies of identified studies were reviewed. The search was up-to-date as of May 2011. Only randomized controlled trials were eligible for inclusion in this review. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies retrieved during the search process. A total of twelve studies were identified, and six of these were selected for further evaluation. One of the studies required translation from Italian. However, none of the studies met the predefined inclusion criteria. An updated search conducted in May 2011 did not identify any additional studies. Based on the currently available literature, no formal recommendations can be made regarding the use of anticholinergic therapy for either acute exacerbations or stable bronchiectasis.
